newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ex-spymasters back alleged East Bloc agent Hernu.
newsitem.headline: Ex-spymasters back alleged East Bloc agent Hernu.

text.p: Former spymasters and a colleague of France's late Socialist politician Charles Hernu cast doubt on Wednesday over a magazine report that the ex-defence minister had been an east bloc agent early in his career.
But several, including Socialist former finance minister Jacques Delors, called for an inquiry to find out what if anything Hernu, who died in 1990, allegedly supplied his Communist patrons.

The weekly L'Express reported that Hernu, defence minister from 1981 to 1985 under Socialist president Francois Mitterrand, was an agent of the Soviet Union and other east bloc countries in the 1950s and 1960s.

The magazine said Hernu was first recruited as a rising political star by a Bulgarian spy in Paris in 1953, and was paid by Bulgaria, Romania and the Soviet Union for at least a decade for supplying reports about French politics.
L'Express said Mitterrand was told in 1992 by French DST counter-intelligence chief Jacques Fournet of the payments. Mitterrand ordered the scandal covered up as a state secret.
"I'm stunned, I knew nothing about this, like all the French people," Delors, finance minister from 1981 to 1984, told Europe-1 radio.

Asked whether the charges rang true, he answered: "For the moment, no, given what I know of him. I understand the shouts of protest from all his friends, all those who worked with him, and his children.
"We should find out whether (his alleged reports) were reports on Paris establishment circles, or state secrets," he added.
Yves Bonnet, DST head in 1982-85, said Hernu may have been approached by east bloc agents early in his career but this should not overshadow later periods of his life.

"In managing the defence ministry, Hernu showed each time that it was necessary the greatest firmness not only towards the Soviet Union but also towards the head of the (French) Communist Party (Georges Marchais)," Bonnet said.

"The accusation is very surprising," echoed Pierre Marion, former head of the DGSE secret service, which answers to the Defence Ministry. "Hernu was pretty much anti-Soviet, anti-Communist. But if there is precise evidence, it should be examined."

Patrice Hernu, one of the late minister's sons, urged President Jacques Chirac to shed light on the affair and added that he may file a suit against what he called "a fabrication coarsely sown together".
The magazine said a record of the payments to Hernu, known by the codenames of "Andre" or "Dinu", was handed to France by an East Bloc country after the 1989 fall of the Berlin Wall.
L'Express said it was unknown whether Hernu had acted for Moscow and its satellites after he became defence minister.

L'Express said Hernu had been paid monthly sums of several thousand francs (hundreds of dollars) for his work, including portraits of politicians like Mitterrand. And in 1958 he accepted the equivalent of 300,000 francs ($60,000) to fund an election campaign to parliament. Hernu lost despite the cash.

Hernu resigned in disgrace from the Defence Ministry in 1985 after French agents sank the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior in Auckland harbour, New Zealand, as the vessel was preparing to protest against French nuclear testing in the South Pacific.
